title: India Tells Bangladesh to Verify 2,860 Nationals for Deportation. Bangladesh Says India Is Pushing People Across the Border.
excerpt: A bilateral mechanism exists on paper. In practice, 2,860 verification requests sit unanswered while both sides trade accusations across a 4,000-kilometre frontier.
body:
India has pressed Bangladesh to expedite the nationality verification of more than 2,860 suspected Bangladeshi nationals believed to be living illegally in the country, even as Dhaka accuses Indian authorities of physically pushing people across the border — a charge New Delhi has not directly denied.

Speaking at the Ministry of External Affairs' weekly press briefing on Thursday, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed that India has sent multiple verification requests to Bangladesh, many of which remain unanswered. "We have many of these requests which are still pending with the Bangladeshi side," Jaiswal said, adding that India expected them to be "expedited as soon as possible so that the deportation of people who are illegally staying in India can be taken forward smoothly and efficiently."

The exchange marks the latest chapter in a deepening diplomatic friction between the two neighbours over illegal immigration, border security, and the treatment of undocumented migrants — issues that have acquired sharper edges since the fall of Sheikh Hasina's government and the deterioration of bilateral ties.

## The Mechanism and Its Failures

On paper, India and Bangladesh have a bilateral deportation mechanism. India refers cases to Bangladesh for nationality verification. Once confirmed, the deportation process moves forward through established channels. In practice, the system has been slow to the point of dysfunction. Jaiswal acknowledged that many requests have been pending for months, without specifying how long.

The bottleneck matters because India's Ministry of Home Affairs set a 30-day deadline earlier this year for states to "detect, identify, and deport illegal immigrants," triggering crackdowns by several BJP-run state governments. Bengali-speaking Muslim migrant workers have been disproportionately affected. Human Rights Watch documented cases of hundreds of Muslims being expelled without adequate verification, including Rohingya refugees in Assam who were pushed across the border.

## Bangladesh's Counter-Accusation

Dhaka is not simply absorbing the pressure. On Thursday, the Border Guard Bangladesh reported that it had foiled ten attempted border infringements by Indian authorities along several stretches of the 4,096-kilometre frontier over the previous 24 hours. The BGB described these as attempts to force people into Bangladesh — what officials have termed "push-ins."

Bangladesh's Foreign Ministry had flagged the issue as early as May, calling the push-ins "unacceptable" and stating that it would "only accept individuals confirmed as Bangladeshi citizens and repatriated through proper channels." India has not publicly responded to the specific push-in allegations.

The dynamic places both governments in an uncomfortable position. India wants faster verification so it can proceed with formal deportations. Bangladesh wants the process to follow established legal channels, not the informal and sometimes violent expulsions that have been documented along the border. Neither side has a political incentive to compromise.

## The Hadi Case Looms Over Everything

The deportation standoff unfolds against the backdrop of the Sharif Osman Hadi murder case, which has become a flashpoint in India-Bangladesh relations. Hadi, a prominent student leader and vocal India critic who helped lead Bangladesh's 2024 mass uprising, was shot in Dhaka in December 2025 and later died in Singapore. Two suspects in his killing are in Indian custody after fleeing through the West Bengal border.

Former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee recently alleged that Indian Home Minister Amit Shah asked her to suppress information about the suspects' arrest — a claim that triggered a complaint against her for breaching official secrecy and linking the Indian government to a "political killing in Bangladesh." Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Shama Obaed, dismissed Banerjee's remarks as statements from a "defeated opposition politician" but confirmed that Dhaka is seeking the suspects' extradition through diplomatic channels.

The convergence of the deportation dispute and the Hadi case has made the border a site of competing narratives. For India, the issue is illegal immigration and the rule of law. For Bangladesh, it is sovereignty and the right to due process. For the millions who live and work on both sides of one of the world's longest and most porous land frontiers, the consequences are immediate and personal.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

The India-Bangladesh border is not an abstraction for NRI communities. Many Indian-origin families in the US, UK, and Gulf states maintain connections on both sides of the frontier. The crackdown on undocumented Bengali-speaking workers, the Hadi murder case, and the broader deterioration of bilateral ties all feed into a narrative of instability that affects remittance flows, family visits, and the political positioning of diaspora communities on South Asian affairs.

The immediate question is whether Bangladesh will accelerate the verification process or continue to treat it as a pressure point in a broader diplomatic negotiation. The answer will shape not just the fate of 2,860 individuals, but the trajectory of a relationship that has been trending downward since August 2024.
